title: Does Weight Decay Enhance Training Stability?
claim: Regularization slows the rise of curvature and stabilizes it well below the classical theoretical threshold.
layout: single wide line plot, left-to-right, dashed horizontal threshold line
description: A single wide line chart. The x-axis is training step (0 to 10000) and the y-axis is sharpness (about 10 to 110). A blue curve for gamma=0 rises steeply from about 12, crosses the dashed gray horizontal line at 100 around step 3000, then hovers slightly above it with small noisy oscillations. A red curve for gamma=0.02 rises much more slowly. It reaches about 80 by step 8000 and plateaus there, clearly below the dashed line. A boxed legend at lower right labels the two curves. Light dashed gridlines sit behind the curves. The eye goes first to the blue curve hitting the dashed threshold, then to the red curve plateauing lower.
caption: The evolution of the sharpness for varying weight decay values γ on an MLP with ReLU activations trained with step size η = 0.02. Weight decay reduces progressive sharpening strength and shrinks the stabilization level significantly below the expected 2
abstract: In modern deep learning, weight decay is often credited with "stabilizing" training dynamics, diverging from its classical role as a static regularization penalty. We investigate a fundamental question: *does weight decay stabilize training dynamics, and if so, through which mechanism?* Indeed, training stability is understood through different but related notions in the literature. We consider how weight decay affects the parameter-space dynamics and loss sharpness by analyzing its effects at the \emph{Edge of Stability} (EoS). We show that weight decay robustly slows *progressive sharpening}. Furthermore, we uncover a striking architecture-dependent phase transition. In CNNs, weight decay dampens the oscillations at the EoS, while in MLPs, increasing weight decay causes a phase transition in which the sharpness stabilizes at a threshold significantly below the theoretical $\frac{2}Î·$ boundary. We develop a mathematical framework that accurately models these phenomena and identify the global alignment of the parameter vector and the sharpness gradient as the mechanistic driver of the phase transition. Importantly, we show that these phenomena translate into stability in terms of search in function-space (NTK). Last, this shows that curvature thresholds obtained from convex/quadratic heuristics may not be reliable stability diagnostics under regularization.
